k-1.x_notes: Strengths: ten problems on five pages, all mathematically correct (traps at multiples of 3 for {1,2}, multiples of 4 for {1,2,3}, 1,4,7,... for misere; Ben's greedy start wins only from 5, 8, 11; the {1,3} game splits by odd/even; two-pile set includes the surprising (1,4) second-player win). The 1-20 trap grids have dot pictures in every cell and small icons of the allowed takes, so kindergartners can count instead of reading numerals to 20. Problem 4 (3, 6, 9 shown twice; cross out each reply the other player could make, circle your answer) puts the outline's 'answer every reply' idea into concrete form at K-1 level. Problem 9 adds a contrasting rule ({1,3}) before the misere twist, and Problem 8 ('find a way to win every time, and show the adult') gives a clear action. Clean format, no fluff. Weaknesses: Problem 4 never says that the two copies stand for the two possible replies, so the adult has to explain it. Three 1-20 trap grids is a lot of classifying for kindergartners. Problem 1 calls for piles of 1 to 6 and 7 to 12 in a way that slightly overlaps with Problem 3.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: the same core sequence (piles 1-5, first/second for 6-9, bigger piles 10-12, traps 1-20, Ben's greedy start, {1,2,3} traps, two piles, mirror strategy with 6+6, misere), and all of it is correct. Problem 6, listing every way a game of 4 and of 5 can go (5 and 8 ways), is a concrete idea with enough rows of counters. Clean format. Weaknesses: the 1-20 trap grids show only numerals, with no dots and no reminder of the allowed takes, which makes them less concrete for kindergartners. Problem 6 never asks who wins each game, so the enumeration drifts away from the strategy idea. Problem 3 mostly repeats Problem 2. Testing a strategy against every reply appears only in the mirror problem. There is no contrasting rule beyond {1,2,3}. Problem 9 is posed as a question with no action or recording space for children who cannot write. The last page holds one grid and is otherwise empty.
k-1.reason: X's dot-picture trap grids and its every-reply problem (3/6/9) make the central ideas more concrete and easier to act on for kindergartners, and its {1,3} game gives a real contrasting rule. Y's enumeration problem is nice but drifts off the strategy idea, and its numeral-only grids are harder for this age.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a strong, correct sequence. {1,2} classification. Two claims to test: Lee's mirror-to-3 at 12 is right, and Mo's take-2 from 10 loses to a take of 2. Jo and Kai under {1,3,4}: leaving 7 wins, leaving 8 loses, and the obvious take-4 is the wrong move from 12. Classify 1-20 (losing piles 2, 7, 9, 14, 16). Extend to 30, 50, 61, 100, which rewards finding the period of 7. The parity game {1,3,5}. A two-pile game. An open design problem: invent a rule whose losing piles are the multiples of 5 ({1,2,3,4} plus any non-multiples of 5). Ample writing space. Problem 7 has six pairs, including three equal-size pairs, so its question about which player wins with equal piles rests on several examples, plus the non-obvious (4,1). Weaknesses: the two-pile problem has little room for the written explanation. The page is fairly text-heavy for second graders, though the adult can read it.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Essentially identical to X in Problems 1-6 and 8, with the same correct mathematics and generous workspace. Problem 7 has only four pairs and just one equal-size pair (3,3), yet still asks children to generalize about equal piles. That leaves too little evidence for the conjecture it asks for. Using 'partner' in place of 'the other player' makes no difference.
grades-2-3.reason: The two packets are nearly identical, but X's two-pile problem gives three equal-size examples (and more pairs overall) to support the generalization it asks for, where Y gives only one.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: rich and correct. {1,3,4} classification to 24 and reasoning out 100, 1000, and 2026 (100 is losing; 1000 take 4; 2026 take 1 or 3). Contrasting patterns for {1,2}, {1,2,4} (still multiples of 3), {1,4} (remainders 0 and 2 mod 5), and {1,3,5}. The greedy test: greedy fails in {1,2}, {1,3,4}, and {1,4} and always works in {1,3,5}. Why the period continues. A complete classification with proof: exactly {1,2,3} with any subset of {5,6}, four games. Misere comparison ({1,3,4} misere losers 1, 3, 8, 10, 15, 17 are a shift of the normal ones). Two-pile grids. In the {1,3,4} two-pile grid the answers are (1,3), (1,8), (3,8), (2,7), and (4,6). Problem 10 generalizes to the pigeonhole argument for any rule with moves up to 4, which is the outline's key periodicity idea. The strips leave empty boxes below the numbers, which suits shading. Weaknesses: ten problems is more than three children will finish in 40 minutes, so Problem 10 serves as a ceiling. Problem 10 partly overlaps Problem 5.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Problems 1-9 are identical to X, with the same correct and substantial mathematics and usable grids. The numbers sit inside the shading boxes, which is workable. There is no general periodicity or pigeonhole problem. The only treatment of why patterns repeat is the specific {1,3,4} case in Problem 5, so the outline's general repeating-pattern argument is missing for a fast fifth grader.
grades-4-5.reason: Same nine problems, but X adds the general pigeonhole periodicity problem, which is the deepest idea in the outline and gives the strongest child somewhere to go.

overall.reason: The packets share most of their material, and all of it is mathematically sound. In every band, X is the same or slightly better. The biggest gap is in K-1, where X's dot-picture grids, every-reply problem, and contrasting {1,3} game are more concrete and closer to the outline. X also adds better two-pile examples for grades 2-3 and the general periodicity problem for grades 4-5.
